newsitem.title: FRANCE: Controversy rages in France over immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: Controversy rages in France over immigration bill.

text.p: Controversy raged in France on Saturday over protests called by intellectuals and leftists against a conservative government bill to crack down on illegal immigration.

As protesters gathered for a 1400 gmt march through central Paris, young members of the ruling Gaullist party handed out leaflets saying the protests no longer had any reason since the bill's most disputed clause had been removed.

But the dispute over the excised clause -- that would have obliged French hosts to notify the police when foreign guests from developing countries left their homes -- has turned into a wider battle over a four-year-old crackdown on immigration.

"France is not a prison that people cannot enter or leave. The whole approach to immigration must be reviewed," said Gerard Mordillat, one of dozens of film-makers who spearheaded protests with a call for civil disobedience.

The Paris march was a test of public feeling about the ideological battle in which each side accuses the other of playing into the hands of anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Front.
The dispute flared after the Front won control of a fourth southern town, Vitrolles, in a municipal by-election.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, accompanying President Jacques Chirac on an official visit to Bucharest, said he was determined to push the bill through parliament.
"It is by fighting illegal immigration that we will force racism and xenophobia to retreat," he told reporters.
The battle raged in newspapers before being taken out on the streets of the capital and other cities, including Bordeaux where Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor.
The influential Le Monde said the crackdown on immigration and the rise of the National Front were being seen abroad as signs of a mounting xenophobia harming France's image.
"Moral rebellion is always right," the left-wing daily Liberation said, accusing the government of "developing ethnic discrimination that will in the end undermine the Republic".
The conservative daily Le Figaro accused intellectuals of being irresponsible in denying the government the means to control illegal immigration.
It published a survey commissioned by the government showing 67 percent of voters backed the revised bill.
The Sofres opinion poll said 61 percent of 1,000 voters questioned opposed a call for civil disobedience by more than 15,000 filmmakers, actors, academics, writers and professionals.

The dispute has embarrassed the main Socialist opposition party, wary of alienating working-class voters who blame immigration for contributing to acute unemployment. Socialist leader Lionel Jospin planned to stay away from the Paris march, saying he would demonstrate in his southwest home region.
More protests are planned for Tuesday when the bill is due for its final reading in the National Assembly.

The Assembly's legislation committeee, in a bid to rescue the bill, last Thursday passed an amendment to make foreigners on short-term visas, rather then their French hosts, responsible for reporting their own departure to the authorities.
While civil rights groups, film personalities, intellectuals and trade unions called for a softening of immigration regulations, Le Pen demands that they be further stiffened.

He calls for abolition of laws giving immigrants the right of family reunification and giving their children born on French soil a right to French citizenship. He also urges that French and European nationals be given preference in jobs, housing and family allowances.
